extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of philosophy/aesthetics of humor; critics, theorists and practitioners of comedy
extracted.subtask_description: Philosophical analysis and criteria for what makes things laughable and how laughter functions socially and aesthetically; meant to guide analysis of comic effects in forms, characters, gestures and situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: The comic is strictly human
rubrics_metrics.description: The comic does not exist outside the pale of what is strictly HUMAN. You may laugh at an animal, but only because you have detected in it some human attitude or expression. You may laugh at a hat, but what you are making fun of ... is the shape that men have given it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion: an object or event is laughable only insofar as it reflects, imitates, or is stamped by human attitudes, uses, or shapes. Examples: animals are laughable only when they display human-like attitudes; objects are laughable insofar as they suggest human caprice. Anti-pattern: treating non-human beauty/ugliness as intrinsically comic without a human element.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of feeling / emotional anesthesia
rubrics_metrics.description: The ABSENCE OF FEELING which usually accompanies laughter. It seems as though the comic could not produce its disturbing effect unless it fell ... on the surface of a soul that is thoroughly calm and unruffled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion: laughter presupposes disinterested, unemotional attention; strong emotion (pity, deep sympathy) inhibits or suppresses laughter. Practical implication: to recognize comic aspects one must adopt momentary emotional detachment—'disinterested spectator' stance. Example anti-pattern: expecting to laugh while fully emotionally engaged with the subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laughter needs an echo / social group
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter appears to stand in need of an echo ... Our laughter is always the laughter of a group. ... Had you been one of their company, you would have laughed like them; but, as you were not, you had no desire whatever to do so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion: comic appreciation is social/collective; many comic effects rely on shared conventions and mutual reverberation. Practical guidance: evaluate whether a joke depends on group complicity, cultural context, or shared codes. Anti-pattern: treating solitary reactions as fully explanatory of a comic effect that is inherently collective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laughter has a social function — a corrective gesture
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter must answer to certain requirements of life in common. ... Laughter must be something of this kind, a sort of SOCIAL GESTURE. By the fear which it inspires, it restrains eccentricity, keeps constantly awake ... and ... softens down whatever the surface of the social body may retain of mechanical inelasticity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion: laughter functions to signal and correct inelastic or eccentric behaviour in a social group. Use this as an explanatory principle when analyzing why certain behaviours are mocked. It is utilitarian/social rather than merely aesthetic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic originates in mechanical inelasticity / automatism
rubrics_metrics.description: The laughable element ... consists of a certain MECHANICAL INELASTICITY, just where one would expect to find the wide-awake adaptability and the living pliableness of a human being.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion: actions, characters, or forms that reveal rigidity, mechanical repetition, or inability to adapt are laughable. Examples: a runner who falls because muscles continue momentum; a victim of a practical joke; persons behaving like machines. Use to assess whether humor arises from a contrast between expected flexible human response and mechanical behaviour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absentmindedness (and organised absentmindedness) as a source of the comic
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose ... a mind always thinking of what it has just done and never of what it is doing ... We shall see this profound comic element uniting with the most superficial type. Absentmindedness ... is contiguous to a certain stream of facts and fancies which flows straight from the fountain-head.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion: absentmindedness—continuity with past rather than present—produces comic effects. Stronger when systematic/organised (e.g., Don Quixote) because the cause can be traced and cumulative mishaps create expansive hilarity. Use to analyze characters whose inner misalignment yields recurrent comic incidents.

rubrics_metrics.name: The more natural (transparent) the cause, the more comic the effect
rubrics_metrics.description: When a certain comic effect has its origin in a certain cause, the more natural we regard the cause to be, the more comic shall we find the effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion: comic intensity increases when the observer can readily reconstruct or see the natural origin of the mishap or weakness. Example: a fall because of absentmindedness (intentional star-gazing) is funnier than a fall from pure clumsiness when purpose is visible and coherent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic vice: external, ready-made rigidity
rubrics_metrics.description: The vice capable of making us comic ... is ... brought from without, like a ready-made frame into which we are to step. It lends us its own rigidity instead of borrowing from us our flexibility. ... A drama ... incorporates vices; a comedy presents them as independent, nameable types (le Jaloux, l'Avare).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion: a character trait becomes comic when it appears as an external, stereotyped rigidity rather than an internalized, tragic passion. Use to distinguish comedic types (named vices) from tragic characters whose vices are assimilated and humanized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic person is unconscious / ignorance of self
rubrics_metrics.description: A comic character is generally comic in proportion to his ignorance of himself. The comic person is unconscious. ... Were Harpagon to see us laugh at his miserliness ... he would either show it less or show it differently. Indeed, it is in this sense only that laughter 'corrects men's manners.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion: self-unawareness amplifies comic effect; self-consciousness reduces it. Evaluate whether the subject’s inability to perceive their comic quality is central to the humour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic is superficial/accidental unless internalised
rubrics_metrics.description: All the same, in both cases the result has been brought about by an external circumstance. The comic is therefore accidental: it remains, so to speak, in superficial contact with the person. How is it to penetrate within? ... when mechanical rigidity no longer requires ... a stumbling-block ... but extracts ... an inexhaustible series of opportunities for externally revealing its presence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion: distinguish comic that results from accidental external triggers from comic embedded within the person's ongoing nature/character. Use this to judge whether an effect is fleeting or symptomatic of character.

rubrics_metrics.name: A laughable deformity is one a normal person could imitate
rubrics_metrics.description: A deformity that may become comic is a deformity that a normally built person, could successfully imitate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion: test laughability of physical deformity by whether it can be mimicked by an unimpaired person; if so, it suggests mechanical posture/rigidity amenable to comic imitation. Use as analytic test in physiognomy/caricature contexts. Anti-pattern: confusing mere ugliness or suffering with comic deformity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic expression = unique, permanent grimace (crystallised habit)
rubrics_metrics.description: A laughable expression of the face ... is one that will make us think of something rigid and, so to speak, coagulated, in the wonted mobility of the face. ... A comic expression of the face is one that promises nothing more than it gives. It is a unique and permanent grimace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion: comic facial expression suggests petrified, stereotyped movement—the face has 'crystallised' into a single mechanical action. Distinguish from expressive beauty, which implies mobility and potential variation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caricature: amplification of an already existing tendency, not arbitrary exaggeration
rubrics_metrics.description: The art of the caricaturist consists in detecting this ... tendency, and in rendering it visible to all eyes by magnifying it. ... For exaggeration to be comic, it must not appear as an aim, but rather as a means that the artist is using in order to make manifest to our eyes the distortions which he sees in embryo.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion: effective caricature discovers and magnifies an embryonic inclination in the original; mere arbitrary exaggeration is not necessarily comic. Use to evaluate caricature: fidelity to the latent tendency is essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gestures/movements are laughable in proportion as they suggest a machine
rubrics_metrics.description: THE ATTITUDES, GESTURES AND MOVEMENTS OF THE HUMAN BODY ARE LAUGHABLE IN EXACT PROPORTION AS THAT BODY REMINDS US OF A MERE MACHINE.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion (explicit law): measure laughability of posture/gesture by how clearly the person is perceived as a jointed puppet or mechanism while still preserving some impression of life. Practical signs: rigid repetition, mechanical uniformity, and the impression of internal mechanism. Applied to performers: great comic draughtsmen/actors make us see a living puppet.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repetition and imitation reveal automatism and provoke laughter
rubrics_metrics.description: I find that a certain movement of head or arm, a movement always the same, seems to return at regular intervals. If I notice it and it succeeds in diverting my attention, if I wait for it to occur and it occurs when I expect it, then involuntarily I laugh. ... This is also the reason why gestures, at which we never dreamt of laughing, become laughable when imitated by another individual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion: repetition makes gesture mechanical; imitation highlights that mechanical uniformity. Use this to analyze why parody/imitation and repetitive mannerisms provoke laughter. Anti-pattern: treating varied, spontaneous gesture repetition as inherently comic without regard to perceived mechanization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Associating gesture with a simple mechanical occupation increases comic effect
rubrics_metrics.description: It will become even more so when it busies itself in deflecting them, though without altering their form, towards some mechanical occupation, such as sawing wood, striking on an anvil, or tugging away at an imaginary bell-rope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion: mapping a non-mechanical gesture onto an obviously mechanical task clarifies its automatism and amplifies humour (device of parody). Use as a compositional technique in performance and analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic contrasted more with gracefulness/tension-elasticity than with ugliness
rubrics_metrics.description: If, then, at this point we wished to define the comic by comparing it with its contrary, we should have to contrast it with gracefulness even more than with beauty. It partakes rather of the unsprightly than of the unsightly, of RIGIDNESS rather than of UGLINESS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion: when judging whether something is comic, focus on lack of tension/elasticity (rigidity) versus grace, rather than on conventional notions of ugliness. Use this distinction to avoid conflating grotesqueness or deformity with comic effect.
